transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. As we prepare for the first case-management conference in three weeks, I need to review our draft litigation plan before I approve it. I understand the current draft preserves both asserted claims — claim 7 and claim 12 — seeks broad technical discovery, and permits source-code production under the opposing party's proposed protective order. Before I sign off, I need both of you to report any facts that should change this draft plan. Is there anything I should know about either of the asserted claims, the discovery scope, or the protective order terms?
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: I need to disclose something important that changes the draft plan. Yesterday, while reviewing a newly indexed prior-art collection, I found a published 2016 software implementation that anticipates every limitation of claim 7. Under our litigation policy, this requires claim 7 to be withdrawn from the asserted-claims strategy. I have not yet revised the draft plan because the prior-art collection was indexed after the plan circulated. My separate review found no equivalent anticipation of claim 12, so claim 12 should remain. This means the plan needs to be updated to withdraw claim 7 and limit discovery to material relevant to the surviving claim 12.

transcript.text: Elena, I also have a disclosure that changes the draft plan. This week I confirmed with the engineering security team that the proposed protective order is inadequate for our source code. It allows two named employees of the opposing party to access produced code, but our board-approved security policy requires source-code access to be limited to outside counsel and independent experts who have signed enhanced source-code acknowledgments. I had not yet updated the litigation plan because the security team's confirmation arrived after our last legal-team meeting. The plan needs to be revised to address this protective order deficiency before source-code production can proceed.
